root_cause.text: The mlx5e TC peer-flow deletion code in en_tc.c incorrectly assumed every index up to MLX5_MAX_PORTS had a valid devcom peer/eswitch, so it iterated over non-existent peer slots and dereferenced NULL peer flow state during cleanup.
root_cause.evidence: The fix replaces `for (i = 0; i < MLX5_MAX_PORTS; i++)` loops in `mlx5e_tc_del_fdb_peers_flow()` and `mlx5e_tc_clean_fdb_peer_flows()` with `mlx5_devcom_for_each_peer_entry(...)`, and the commit message explicitly says to "iterate only over actual devcom peers instead of assuming all possible ports exist" to avoid "touching non-existent peers"; the crash occurs in `mlx5e_tc_del_fdb_peers_flow` with a NULL pointer dereference.

intent_record.intent_summary: Fix peer FDB flow deletion to iterate over actual devcom peer eswitches instead of all possible port indices.
intent_record.what: The function mlx5e_tc_del_fdb_peers_flow() was changed from iterating over all port indices from 0 to MLX5_MAX_PORTS and skipping the local device index, to instead declare devcom, pos, and peer_esw variables, fetch devcom from flow->priv->mdev->priv.eswitch->devcom, iterate over peer eswitch entries with mlx5_devcom_for_each_peer_entry(devcom, peer_esw, pos), derive i from mlx5_get_dev_index(peer_esw->dev), and call mlx5e_tc_del_fdb_peer_flow(flow, i) for each discovered peer.
intent_record.how: At runtime, peer flow deletion now targets only actual peer eswitch devices registered in devcom instead of blindly scanning every possible port index except the local one. This avoids attempting deletions for non-existent or unrelated ports and ensures cleanup follows the real peer topology.

intent_record.intent_summary: Use devcom peer enumeration when cleaning FDB peer flows so cleanup runs only for actual peer devices instead of all possible port slots.
intent_record.what: The function mlx5e_tc_clean_fdb_peer_flows() was changed to declare devcom, pos, and peer_esw variables, assign devcom = esw->devcom, remove the for-loop over 0..MLX5_MAX_PORTS with the skip of the local device index, and instead iterate peer devices using mlx5_devcom_for_each_peer_entry(devcom, peer_esw, pos); inside that loop it computes i = mlx5_get_dev_index(peer_esw->dev) before deleting entries from esw->offloads.peer_flows[i].
intent_record.how: At runtime, peer flow cleanup now targets only actual peer devices registered in the devcom group instead of scanning all possible port indices and excluding self. This avoids relying on MLX5_MAX_PORTS/index layout and ensures deletion is performed for real peers that exist, improving correctness of peer flow cleanup in multi-device setups.

candidates.rationale: This loop embodies the faulty assumption that every port index up to MLX5_MAX_PORTS corresponds to a valid peer device. It causes deletion to run for non-existent peers, leading to NULL peer flow state dereferences during cleanup.
This cleanup loop iterates over all possible peer slots instead of only actual devcom peers, directly matching the root cause of traversing invalid peer entries.
Because i may refer to a non-existent peer slot, this statement traverses peer flow lists for invalid/uninitialized peer state, making the NULL dereference during cleanup possible.
This call performs peer-flow deletion using an index produced by the invalid all-ports iteration, so it can dereference missing peer state for non-existent peers.

vuln_statements.explanation: This loop is the core faulty assumption: it iterates across all possible port indices rather than only actual devcom peer eswitches. That causes cleanup to process non-existent peer slots, which leads to NULL peer flow state dereferences.
Using i from the all-ports iteration, this traversal accesses peer flow lists for slots that may not correspond to a real peer. That makes cleanup operate on invalid or uninitialized peer state.
This deletion call consumes the invalid peer index generated by the erroneous iteration, triggering peer-flow cleanup on non-existent peers and enabling the NULL dereference.

bic_trace_step.reason:
The snippet is sufficient because it shows the full cleanup logic introduced by this commit, including both peer-flow deletion helpers and the peer-flow cleanup loop. The vulnerable construct is present in `mlx5e_tc_del_fdb_peers_flow()`:

`for (i = 0; i < MLX5_MAX_PORTS; i++) {`
`    if (i == mlx5_get_dev_index(flow->priv->mdev))`
`        continue;`
`    mlx5e_tc_del_fdb_peer_flow(flow, i);`
`}`

This iterates over every possible port index up to `MLX5_MAX_PORTS`, assuming each index represents a valid peer. But `mlx5e_tc_del_fdb_peer_flow(flow, i)` immediately performs operations on per-peer state without checking that a peer actually exists for that `peer_index`, notably:

`list_del(&flow->peer[peer_index]);`

The root cause says cleanup wrongly assumed every index up to `MLX5_MAX_PORTS` had a valid devcom peer/eswitch and could dereference NULL peer flow state during cleanup. This commit introduces exactly that pattern: unconditional iteration across all possible peer slots and unconditional deletion of `flow->peer[peer_index]` for each slot.

The cleanup entrypoint also reflects the same assumption:

`for (i = 0; i < MLX5_MAX_PORTS; i++) {`
`    if (i == mlx5_get_dev_index(esw->dev))`
`        continue;`
`    list_for_each_entry_safe(flow, tmp, &esw->offloads.peer_flows[i], peer[i])`
`        mlx5e_tc_del_fdb_peers_flow(flow);`
`}`

There is no validation here that `i` corresponds to an actually existing peer relationship before invoking peer cleanup across all indices. Therefore the vulnerable construct is present.

The fix is not present in this snippet because there is no guard that limits iteration to actual devcom peers, no existence check for a valid peer/eswitch per index before cleanup, and no conditional protection around `list_del(&flow->peer[peer_index])`. So this commit version contains the bug and does not yet contain the fix.
